text: ethereum:native will be a post-quantum store of value btw

quoted_tweet.author: vitalik.eth
quoted_tweet.text:
3. Optimizing for ETH as SoV is aligned with decentralization and CROPS

Whenever I ask what people appreciate the most about Ethereum (as opposed to either other blockchains, or anything outside the blockchain world), the most common answer is: decentralization and CROPS (censorship and capture resistance, open source, privacy and security).

Decentralization and CROPS have a lot of value, even to institutions. For individuals, privacy is often viewed as an abstract ideology. For institutions, it's prudent risk management, data protection law compliance, and a number of other things. Likewise for security. And likewise for running your own node (enterprise buzzword: "on-prem deployment").

But what about for the ETH holder? Well, it depends why you're an ETH holder. If you want ETH to optimally chase financial trends and collect fees from them, then you want a Fearless Leader™ who bravely shouts on the socials that Ethereum loves [insert opportunity here] and will pragmatically reconfigure itself to give it explicit protocol support.

But if your primary reason to hold ETH is as an SoV, then you will be judging ETH by SoV-ish metrics. And what is the first and most important SoV-ish metric?

To survive.

That's what a big chunk of this last Devcon was about ("post-quantum and post-AI"). You want a chain that is taking conservative tradeoffs ("hash-only security, all formally proven, >3x more rounds than known to be necessary for security"). You want a chain that is aiming for at least partial ossification, where the great balance of work will move to higher levels of the stack once the core is complete. You want a chain that aims to minimize protocol politics, by having a very high bar before it accepts either precompiles that bloat the protocol or new kinds of in-protocol rewards that could get captured.

What other SoV'ish metrics?

The ability to easily hold it safely (hence, work on multisigs).
The ability to hold it privately (hence, kohaku work).
The ability to hold it privately *and* safely (hence, 8288 and private-AA workstreams already starting).
The guarantee that if you have coins, you can send them, and block builders can't stop you (FOCIL)
Minimized infrastructure dependence (basically the whole decentralization roadmap, including the fact that I am able to currently run a node on this laptop, and it synced in < 6 hours and takes up only 1/8 of my hard drive - better stats than in 2019!)

Now, are there "adoption" goals that are highly synergistic with SoV?

Very much so.

The more assets there are natively issued on L1, including both RWAs and native decentralized assets, the larger a set of things you can "do" with your ETH, the better. Being able to easily (including safely, trustlessly) convert back and forth between ETH and other assets, use ETH as collateral to do things with other assets, etc, all forms part of the utility of holding ETH.

There are still some conflicts between serving these use cases and decentralization (eg. we want to be careful about fast slots and impact on centralization), but on the whole much less than what you get if you maximize fees.

Conclusion:

The best social reason to care about Ethereum is because it makes decentralization and CROPS properties a reality for more people and uses.

The best private reason to hold ETH is its SoV properties, which are a direct consequence of that decentralization and CROPS.

text:
A quick take on "we want to be careful about fast slots", as someone who is constantly talking about them :)

I agree, and said as much in my devcon talk (https://youtu.be/zfaghEoRxFs?si=jy-jDVId6pPx5NON&t=888).

Ethereum is not aiming for a slot time that would destroy its unique value proposition.

Ethereum is aiming to reduce its slot time *because* faster slots foster an environment where the network and ethereum:native thrive even further. Being slow is not a virtue. Being fast isn't everything we need to be either, but it is a user- and asset-friendly property of the network, on its own terms.

Let's not forget the positive correlation between shorter slots and censorship-resistance (and even builder market health!) *as long as* these shorter slots are supported by a decentralised network.

We can, and should, aim for everything: Security and utility. They are not at odds. We're not close to the efficient frontier. Let's get all the things!

Expanding on why I believe "ETH as store of value (SoV)" makes much more sense to focus on than "ETH as fee-burning token".

Three primary reasons:

1. ETH as fee-burning token never was as strong as it seemed
2. Optimizing for ETH as fee-burning token would demand Ethereum and ETH function in ways that are very hard to make compatible with decentralization and capture resistance.
3. Meanwhile, optimizing for ETH as SoV is aligned with Ethereum focusing on its unique strengths (decentralization and CROPS)

EIP-1559 (including its burn) is fine and good, we should keep them. But we should not feel sad if fee burn is < 10% of breakeven indefinitely; the value of ETH comes from elsewhere.

The core idea: the big thing that people appreciate about Ethereum is decentralization and CROPS. The main pragmatic benefit that these things translate into is stability. SoV is the category where that is not an unneeded extra we merely put effort into for ideological reasons, but rather a pragmatic strength from the perspective of people putting in their assets. And in the era of AI disruption, stability will be highly valued.

I agree! Lots of pareto improvements.

Top few I see are:

1. DC available chain (current PQ roadmap) only has a few hundred validators in the hot path of each slot. Consensus time ~= log(validator count), so going from 30k vals -> 500 is plausibly a 2x speed boost.
2. Erasure coded P2P improves expected propagation time of big objects with no downside except some code complexity (which is manageable, esp given that this is not consensus code)
3. Few-slot finality. PQ sig aggregation is able to handle a message from every validator per round, and even at very conservative params (eg. ~5 rounds of aggregation, 1m validators) current math/simulations imply finality in under a minute (compare: 2.5 epochs = 16 min avg finality today)

So effectively, significant efficiency gains are part of the (currently understood) PQ security roadmap "for free"

You can sell a website to a business that doesn't have one.

Claude builds it in minutes. You just have to make the call.

A post about a guy closing 54 local businesses in 30 days this way hit 190K views yesterday. We can't verify his $67K. The method is real, so here's how to run it properly.

→ Find them. Google Maps, "[business type] in [city]". Pick the ones with no website or a site from 2012.
→ Never publish a site with their name on it before they say yes. Share a private preview: publish the Claude artifact as a link, or drop the HTML file on Netlify Drop for a free test URL.
→ Expect 1 or 2 yeses out of 10 calls, not 9. Plan for volume.

Prompt 1: Pick who to call first

"Here are 20 businesses from Google Maps with their name, rating, number of reviews and website (or none): [paste]. Rank them by how likely they are to pay for a simple website: busy and well reviewed but no site or an outdated one goes first. For the top 5, write one line on what they're losing without a site."

Prompt 2: Build the demo

"Build a one-page website for a [business type] called [name] in [city]. Phone: [phone]. Address: [address]. What they do: [copy from their Google Maps profile].
- Sections: hero with a clear headline and one call to action, services, why choose us, 3 review quotes marked as placeholders, map and contact form.
- Mobile first, fast, no stock-photo clichés. Use [colors from their logo or storefront].
- Write the copy for their real customers in [city].
- Mark every placeholder in [brackets] so I never show fake reviews or prices as real.
Give me a single HTML file I can preview."

Prompt 3: The call script

"I'm calling the owner of [business]. Open with their problem: people search for them on Google and find nothing, or an outdated site. Then offer to show a free demo I already made. Write a 30-second opener, the 3 objections they'll most likely raise (price, 'I get clients from referrals', 'my nephew does that') with a short honest answer to each, and how to close for a 10-minute screen share. Friendly, no fake urgency."

Our take: Claude made the website the easy part. The money is in the 30 calls you make after lunch.

人类最强模型 Claude Fable 5.2 和 Mythos 5.2 发布。
几乎所有能力都超过了 Opus 5.5 。
这是人类目前最前沿的大模型，没有之一。

一句话简单总结：
人类目前最强模型，价格下降20%，速度提升30%，编程办公不在话下，生物医药和机器人都能搞定。

这是核心信息的快速笔记：
1. 虽然更为智能了，但模型的安全对齐方面，比以往模型都要好或持平（可能使用了他们研究里所说的讲故事对齐法）
2. 几乎所有能力都超过 Opus 5.5，而且沟通风格更加清晰明了
3. 生成速度相比上一代的 5.1 快了 30%
4. 在 FrontierCode 2.0 测试中，Fable 5.2 High 就能打平 Opus 5.5 Max，但每任务成本只要一半。需要注意的是 Fable 5.2 在  Xhigh 时得分最高，比 Max 都高。思考努力程度并非越高越好。
5. 基因疗法可以通过一种称为衣壳的蛋白质外壳进行递送。Mythos 5.2 发现了一种预测整个衣壳结构的新方法。它准确地模拟了其尝试的 34 个衣壳中的 28 个。生物学家可以使用它来更快、更便宜地设计衣壳。
6. 由 1,000 个 Fable 5.2 Agents 组成的团队在 30 小时内完全形式化了费马大定理，将证明翻译成一种计算机可以逐步检查的语言。在相同的设置下，Opus 5.5 在 18 小时内仅完成了 26%，并且在 30 小时后几乎没有取得更多进展。
7. Mythos 5.2 在控制物理机器人方面展现了显著提升的技能，即使是在它从未明确接受过训练的任务上。（和 Astra 一样具备了机器人方面的泛化能力，在其他模型上暂未观察到）在 RoboDojo 上，这是一个带有模拟双臂机器人的基准测试，它超越了其他模型以及大多数专为控制机器人而构建的 AI 系统。
8. 官方建议是，大多数 Coding 和知识任务，建议使用 Opus 5.5 起手，把最具雄心、开放式的技术工作交给 Mythos 和 Fable。
9. 价格方面，8 美元输入，40 美元输出，较之前的 10 美元和 50 美元下降了 20%。

这两个模型是同一个模型的不同版本，Fable 定位更为大众，Mythos 则开放了生物等安全领域。

Every world-changing company starts with someone who sees things differently.  

The Method goes beyond the company to understand the person behind it, how they think, and the future they’re building toward.  

A new @MTSlive original mini-doc series by @sophiadew.

today we launched The Method, an @MTSlive original mini-doc series that tells the story of the founders behind the world’s most important companies.

since joining MTS, I’ve interviewed hundreds of founders. and the biggest lesson I’ve learned is that the best founders are deeply optimistic. when you understand how they think, what motivates them, and why they dedicate their lives to shaping the world, you can’t help but want to do it too. 

a lot of the personal ambitions in my life have come from reading memoirs. I remember reading Shoe Dog, and feeling inspired by how Phil Knight relentlessly pursued what he knew to be true, even though the rest of the world didn't see it yet. when Nike was founded, “personal fitness” wasn’t a thing, working out was a fringe subculture, and people would even spit on runners in the street. then Phil came along and changed the world’s relationship to fitness forever.

even if you don’t personally care about running, Phil’s story was a reminder that the future is malleable and every person has agency to shape it.

today, people are launching rockets and curing cancer. there are no limits to what's possible. information is democratized, the cost of building is practically free, and entrepreneurship is on the rise. It's never been a better time to act on your ambitions. and understanding others who have done so, gives us a blueprint on how to do the same.

a big thank you to all the people who brought The Method to life. MTS is expanding beyond a livestream to a full media network and today marks the start of this new era. first episode airs tomorrow!
